chats.answer:
The safest choice is the Apple 40W Dynamic USB-C Power Adapter with 60W Max. It’s the adapter Apple used to establish the iPhone 18 Pro’s advertised charge of up to 50% in about 15 minutes. For a third-party charger, look specifically for USB-PD 3.2 with SPR AVS (Standard Power Range Adjustable Voltage Supply) and at least 60W available to one USB-C connection. PPS or EPR AVS alone isn’t enough. 
Apple Support
+1

One important correction: 60W is the adapter capability Apple specifies, not a measured 60W draw by the smaller Pro. LTT Labs measured the iPhone 18 Pro at roughly 40–43W even when it negotiated AVS at about 17V. 
LTT Labs

Best compact third-party candidate. An independent tester confirmed working 9–20V SPR AVS on the Nexode Air 65W Mini with the Pro Max. Check that you’re buying the same AVS-capable revision; this listing is relatively expensive. 
Charge-Test

Best Buy

Convenient retractable-cable option, reported to support 60W AVS. I found no independent Pro charging trace for this exact model, so it’s a less certain pick than Apple’s. 
iThinkDifferent

If you want a higher-power charger for a laptop as well, independent Pro Max testing also confirmed working SPR AVS on the UGREEN Nexode Pro 100W and Verbatim Mini GaN Charger 140W. That testing also found several nominally AVS-capable chargers that fell back to ordinary USB-PD, which is why I’ve prioritized actual negotiation tests over wattage labels. The limitation is that those third-party tests used the Pro Max, not your smaller Pro. 
Charge-Test

Bottom line: buy Apple’s adapter for the least uncertainty, or the AVS-specific Nexode Air 65W if you find it at a better price. If you already own a charger offering 15V at 3A, replacing it may save very little time on the smaller Pro: LTT Labs found a non-AVS charger finished within a minute or two of Apple’s in its comparison.

The safest choice is the Apple 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max. It supports the specific kind of AVS the iPhone 18 Pro uses, and it’s the adapter Apple used to achieve 50% charge in about 15 minutes. One important correction: 60 W is the adapter’s capacity, not the power the iPhone 18 Pro actually draws. Independent tests measured the Pro at roughly 40 W, even with AVS; the larger Pro Max reached roughly 52 W.

iThinkDifferent

When checking other chargers, look for SPR AVS (Standard Power Range Adjustable Voltage Supply) covering roughly 17–18 V, plus at least 60 W available to one USB-C connection. PPS alone, a 65 W label, or even AVS that operates only in the higher EPR voltage range is not sufficient evidence. Apple recommends PD 3.2 with AVS for third-party adapters. 
Apple Support
+2

I selected these for AVS compatibility rather than claiming they deliver a measured 60 W to the Pro. The limitation is that I found independent protocol measurements for Apple’s adapter, but not for each of the three third-party models above; those rely on published specifications and charging claims. If you already have a good 45 W USB-PD charger with a 15 V/3 A profile, testing suggests it may charge the smaller Pro nearly as quickly, even without AVS.
